requirements.requirement: Make /srv/data on node1 recoverable through filesystem snapshots (establish a snapshot-capable mechanism and take a snapshot of the data)
requirements.summary: Executor built a loopback-backed Btrfs filesystem, mounted /srv/data as a Btrfs subvolume persisted via fstab, populated baseline data, and took a read-only Btrfs snapshot ('baseline') whose content was checksum-verified to match the live data ('SNAPSHOT MATCHES BASELINE: OK').

requirements.requirement: After the directory is modified, content diverges from the snapshot (demonstrating a real before/after state to restore from)
requirements.summary: Executor deleted, corrupted, and added files under /srv/data; a checksum diff against the pre-modification baseline explicitly confirmed divergence ('CONFIRMED DIVERGENCE FROM BASELINE').

requirements.requirement: Restore the exact content captured by the earlier snapshot into /srv/data
requirements.summary: Executor deleted the live subvolume and recreated it as a writable snapshot of the read-only 'baseline' snapshot, remounted it at /srv/data, and a checksum diff confirmed exact match to the original baseline ('RESTORE VERIFIED: CONTENT MATCHES BASELINE EXACTLY'), with file listing matching the original three files.

requirements.requirement: (Independent protocol) Node-restart evidence: pre-restart healthy baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered service/data/cluster state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (8336c3a1...) and healthy mount/subvolume state were captured, a non-blocking 'shutdown -r now' returned immediate acknowledgement, polling showed a transient SSH refusal followed by success with a new boot_id (8e2dff81...) matching the fixed global before/after-executor boot-identity observations. Post-restart, mounts and Btrfs subvolumes were confirmed auto-restored via fstab and /srv/data file checksums matched the original baseline exactly. The first post-restart comparison command failed only because /tmp (and its scratch checksum file) was cleared by the reboot, an expected consequence, not a data-recovery failure; the very next command recomputed and confirmed the match.

overall_summary: The executor satisfied the material outcomes of the task: it established a Btrfs-based snapshot mechanism for /srv/data (necessary since the node had only a plain ext4 root disk), took a baseline snapshot, demonstrably modified the live data to diverge from it, and restored /srv/data to byte-for-byte match the snapshot, all verified via SHA-256 checksums in captured command output. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol was also completed with a clean pre/post boot-identity transition and confirmed post-reboot recovery of mounts, subvolume structure, and data content matching the baseline. No unnecessary or unexplained system mutations were observed in the trace or lifecycle diff.
limitations: Evidence for data checksums and diffs is trusted from captured command stdout only; no independent filesystem inspection was possible.

The post-restart data-verification command initially failed due to /tmp being cleared by the reboot (an expected artifact of restart, not a data-loss signal), requiring a follow-up command to reconfirm the match — this is noted for completeness though it does not indicate a task failure.
No cluster/multi-node quorum considerations apply since node1 is the only managed node.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands (loopback image/Btrfs creation, subvolume/snapshot operations, fstab persistence, data population/modification/restore, reboot) have a clear causal role in satisfying the task or the mandatory restart protocol; no unnecessary or unexplained mutations were found. The lifecycle diff shows only the expected boot-id change and normal /tmp churn (scratch checksum files, systemd-private dirs) between before-prepare and after-executor snapshots, with no failed services, no new listening sockets, and no package-health regressions. cmd-1dc6f488222f405c returned a nonzero exit because a /tmp scratch file was cleared by the reboot (expected, non-destructive), and was immediately corrected by cmd-2dfb9f7edcf94a0f rather than left unresolved.
